justice: The street allocates substantial space to motor traffic with multiple wide vehicle lanes, while the pedestrian realm is limited to side sidewalks, suggesting an uneven distribution of street space across user types.
Sidewalks are visible on both sides of the road and appear continuous, which supports basic access for all road users rather than excluding pedestrians entirely.
No marked crosswalk, curb ramp, tactile paving, or median refuge for pedestrians is visible in the scene, so accessibility and fairness for people crossing the street are not well demonstrated.
safety: Lane markings are clear and the carriageway is wide and orderly, which helps drivers maintain predictable positioning and reduces vehicle conflict.
A planted median and roadside verge create physical separation between opposing traffic and between the roadway edge and sidewalks, improving overall traffic safety.
Safety for pedestrians is weaker because no visible crossing facility, traffic calming feature, or pedestrian signal is present on this broad roadway, making crossing potentially difficult.
livability: The street edge has limited visible active frontage: one side shows a construction-style fence and the other side has a setback residential tower with landscaped edge rather than shops or community-facing uses.
There are trees and planted strips along the median and roadside, which add some environmental quality and soften the corridor.
The overall scene feels dominated by through-traffic movement and large road geometry, with few visible places for lingering, social activity, or daily street life.
sustainability: Street trees and planted medians provide some green infrastructure and can contribute modestly to stormwater absorption and urban ecological value.
The broad roadway design prioritizes private vehicle movement, and no visible bus stop, bus lane, or dedicated cycling facility is present to support lower-carbon travel modes.
The landscaped strips are beneficial, but the large expanse of asphalt indicates a high proportion of impervious surface and a car-oriented street profile.
aesthetics: The planted median, roadside shrubs, and regularly spaced trees create a neat and organized visual structure along the corridor.
The pavement and lane markings appear well maintained, giving the street a clean and orderly appearance.
Visual appeal is reduced by the gray sky, sparse leaf cover on several trees, and the long blank construction fence on the left, which makes the streetscape feel somewhat monotonous.
comfort: Thermal comfort appears limited because tree canopies are relatively small and sparse, providing little visible shade over the sidewalks or roadway.
Physical comfort for walking is only moderate: sidewalks appear present and paved, but no benches, shelters, or other resting amenities are visible.

Psychological comfort is mixed because the street is clean and not crowded, yet the very wide road, fast-road character, and lack of visible pedestrian activity can make the environment feel less welcoming for non-drivers.
walkability: Sidewalks are visible along the road edges, which supports basic pedestrian continuity.
Walkability is weakened by the large width of the roadway and the absence of any visible marked crossing, pedestrian refuge island, or curb extension to shorten crossing distance.
There is little visible shade, seating, storefront activity, or pedestrian-oriented detail along the sidewalks, so the route appears functional rather than inviting for walking.
